extracted.intended_audience: inventors and practitioners preparing and filing U.S. design patent applications (applicants, patent agents/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing, filing, and prosecuting United States design patent applications, including required elements (specification, drawings/photos, claim, oath), drawing standards, prosecution practice, and procedural/formal requirements. Focused on compliance with USPTO rules, MPEP guidance, and relevant statutes/regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a design
rubrics_metrics.description: A design consists of the visual ornamental characteristics embodied in, or applied to, an article of manufacture; it may relate to configuration/shape, surface ornamentation, or their combination. When the design is only surface ornamentation, the ornamentation is inseparable from the article and must be shown applied to an article of manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that design patents protect appearance (ornamentality) rather than function; surface ornamentation must be shown applied to an article and the article should be graphically distinguished (e.g., broken lines). See MPEP references linked in the guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of designs and modified forms (entire article, portion, surface ornamentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ornamental design may be embodied in an entire article, only a portion of an article, or ornamentation applied to an article. If directed to surface ornamentation only, the article must be shown (typically in broken lines) and a statement explaining that broken lines form no part of the claimed design must be added to the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs that are independent and distinct must be filed in separate applications; modified forms/embodiments of a single design concept may be filed together if not patentably distinct (examples: minimal configuration differences). Use broken lines or other techniques to graphically distinguish the article from the ornamentation and include required explanatory statements in the specification. See MPEP 1504.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single claim requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent application must include only a single claim (37 CFR § 1.153).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because only one claim is permitted, distinct or independent designs (no apparent relationship, or different shapes/appearances) must be filed in separate applications. Modified embodiments of a single design concept that are not patentably distinct may be included in the same application (example: vases with minimal configuration differences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper subject matter for design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to pictures/prints/etc. per se (not applied to an article) are improper. A design dictated primarily by function lacks ornamentality and is not proper subject matter. A design that simulates a well-known or naturally occurring object/person is not 'original.' Subject matter offensive to protected groups is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 35 U.S.C. 171 and MPEP 1504.01 (including 1504.01(c) and 1504.01(d)) and MPEP 608 and 37 CFR § 1.3. Evaluate whether appearance is dictated by function (no alternative designs) and whether design is original; exclude offensive material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between design and utility patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility patents protect how an article is used and works (35 U.S.C. 101) while design patents protect appearance (35 U.S.C. 171). An article may be eligible for both if it has both functional and ornamental features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the distinct legal protections and consider whether design protection alone will achieve the applicant's goals; see MPEP 1502.01 for overlap considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protecting designs outside the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. design patent rights extend only within the United States; applicants wishing protection abroad must apply in each country/region or use the Hague Agreement international design application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For inventions made in the U.S., a foreign filing license from the USPTO Director is required before filing abroad; filing a U.S. application serves as a request. Consult MPEP 2900 and MPEP 140 and specific foreign laws to avoid loss of rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of a design patent application (required papers)
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent application should include: design application transmittal, fee transmittal, application data sheet (per 37 CFR § 1.76), specification, drawings or photographs, and the inventor's oath or declaration (37 CFR § 1.153(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow USPTO forms (PTO/AIA/18, PTO/SB/17, PTO/AIA/14, PTO/AIA/01 or PTO/AIA/08). The guide suggests following the presented formats to ensure completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification sections and order
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should include, where applicable and in order: preamble, cross-reference to related applications, statement regarding federally sponsored research, description of the figure(s) of the drawing, feature description, and a single claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section headings in uppercase without underlining or bold should precede each section. Sample specifications and disclosure examples are provided in the guide. See 37 CFR 1.154 for arrangement guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble and title requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The preamble should state applicant name, title of the design, and a brief description of the nature and intended use of the article in which the design is embodied. The title must identify the article by the name generally known and used by the public; marketing designations are improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specific, descriptive title aids examiner search/classification and public understanding. See MPEP 1503.01 for additional guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figure descriptions and permissible descriptive statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Figure descriptions should indicate what each view represents (front elevation, top plan, perspective, etc.). Generally the drawing is the best description; additional descriptive statements are permissible when useful (e.g., mirror image, portions not shown do not form part of the claimed design, purpose of broken lines, nature/intended use if not in preamble).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use descriptive statements sparingly and only to clarify aspects not evident in drawings. Examples of permissible statements are provided in the guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal claim language and incorporation of drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: The single claim must identify the subject as the 'ornamental design' and indicate the article of manufacture and incorporate the drawings. Claim form: 'The ornamental design for (the article which embodies the design) as shown.' If descriptive statement included, add 'and described.' The article designation should match the title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claim must be in formal terms; see MPEP 1503.01(III) for more information. Accurate claim wording ties the scope to the drawings and any descriptive statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings or photographs are the critical disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Every design patent application must include a drawing or photograph of the claimed design. The drawings/photographs constitute the entire visual disclosure of the claim and must be clear and complete; nothing should be left to conjecture. They must comply with 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, and include sufficient views to completely disclose the appearance of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poor or incomplete drawings may render the disclosure fatally defective and nonenable. It is recommended to use a professional draftsperson. Changing drawings after filing to add new matter is prohibited (35 U.S.C. 132; 35 U.S.C. 112(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographs and ink drawings usage rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs and ink drawings may be included in the same application, but they must not be used to disclose the same embodiment. Photographs used in lieu of ink drawings are limited to showing the article and must exclude the article’s environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using both for the same embodiment risks inconsistencies between elements. Follow 37 CFR § 1.84(b)(1) and § 1.152 and the guide's examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black-and-white drawing/photo standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings are normally required to be in black ink on white paper. Black-and-white photographs are permitted subject to 37 CFR § 1.84(b)(1) and § 1.152. Electronic submission of black-and-white line drawings and photographs is allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Black-and-white photographs on double weight photographic paper must show figure numbers on the face; mounted photos may show figure number on Bristol board. See MPEP 502.05 for electronic filing legal guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color drawings and color photographs rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Color drawings/photographs are permitted if filed according to 37 CFR § 1.84(a)(2) and § 1.84(b)(2). If color is included, one set of color drawings/photographs is required for e-filing or three sets if not e-filed, and the specification must include language noting color in the file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If color is integral to the claimed design, omission of color later is permitted only if underlying configuration is clear. If color is not part of the claim, include the statement: 'The color shown on the claimed design forms no part thereof.' Petitions are no longer required for color; examples and required wording are in the guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Views required to disclose a design (sufficient number of views)
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings or photographs should include enough views to completely disclose the appearance, typically front, rear, right/left sides, top and bottom; perspective views are suggested for three-dimensional designs. Combinations of plan, elevation and perspective views may help ensure completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If sides are identical/mirror images, one side view plus a statement may suffice; bottom may be omitted with a statement that it is flat and unornamented. Some non-visible sides during normal use may be omitted. Sectional views are permissible only to show external appearance. See MPEP 1503.02(I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface shading requirements and cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Surface shading is not required but may be necessary to show character/contour and to distinguish open and solid areas. Solid black shading is permitted only to show the color black or color contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of appropriate surface shading may render the drawing nonenabling and indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(a)/(b). Adding surface shading after filing may be considered new matter. See MPEP 1503.02(II) and MPEP 608.04 for new matter concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broken lines usage and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Anything not part of the claimed design may be shown in broken lines (environment, bounds, article when claim is only surface ornamentation). Broken lines should not interfere with clear understanding and should be lighter than lines of the claimed design. Broken lines may not be used to show hidden planes/surfaces which cannot be seen through opaque materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When broken lines are used, the specification must explicitly identify their purpose so the scope of the claim is clear. If broken lines obscure the claimed design, provide an unobscured separate figure. See MPEP 1503.02(III). Include a statement when the article form shown in broken lines forms no part of the claimed design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing shading types and limitations (stippling vs straight-line)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common shading techniques include straight-line surface shading and stippling; they may be used individually or in combination but should not be used together on the same surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both can represent character/contour and surface contrast. Use consistent shading conventions; the guide provides visual examples. Avoid mixing shading methods on the same surface to prevent confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent materials depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Oblique line shading must be used to show transparent or translucent surfaces (and highly polished/reflective surfaces). Elements visible behind transparent surfaces should be shown in light, full lines, not broken lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct depiction ensures clarity about what is part of the claimed design versus what is background or internal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploded views and brackets
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploded views are only supplementary to a fully assembled view; a bracket must be used to show association of elements in an exploded view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploded views cannot replace a fully assembled view; use them only to supplement and clarify relationships among elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate positions and separate views
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternate positions of a design or an element must be shown in separate views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to show alternate positions in the same view; provide separate figures for each position to disclose the variation clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article shown broken away guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: A separation and bracket may be used in an enlarged view when full length of the article is shown in another view. Alternatively, when the article is consistently shown with a break, the claim is understood to be directed only to the portions shown between break lines; the specification must explain that appearance of portions between breaks forms no part of the claimed design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit description in specification to avoid ambiguity about scope when broken-away or truncated views are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-sectional view limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-sections may be used to clarify disclosure and minimize number of views, but sectional views presented to show strictly interior construction or functional/mechanical features are unnecessary and may confuse the scope of the claimed design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sectional views only to clarify external appearance relevant to the design; avoid sections that suggest interior/functional claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple embodiments in one application
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple embodiments of a single concept may be filed in one design application so long as their appearance and shape are similar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure embodiments are not patentably distinct; similarity in appearance/shape is required. Examples are provided in the guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphic drawing symbols and legends
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphic drawing symbols and labeled representations may be used for conventional elements where appropriate, subject to Office approval. Legends or ANSI/ISO symbols may be used but the Office will not approve a published collection of symbols as a group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overly specific or unclear symbols; symbols should not interfere with a clear showing of the design. Because color may now be filed, applicants may prefer color drawings rather than pictorial symbols to indicate color. See 37 CFR § 1.84(n) and MPEP 1503.02 V and MPEP 608.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols to indicate materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain symbols should be used to indicate various materials where the material is an important feature of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conventional material symbols aid prior art searches. Use symbols judiciously and label unclear symbols for clarification; consider ANSI/ISO standards as guides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath or declaration requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: An oath or declaration is required in non-provisional applications. Use form PTO/AIA/01 (preferred) or PTO/AIA/08; declaration may be submitted in lieu of an oath. The oath/declaration must include required statements (original inventor, authorized application) and provide legal name and mailing address (if not in ADS). Substitute statements are available for deceased/incapacitated/unreachable/refusing inventors under specified limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oaths must be notarized; declarations need not. Substitute statement form PTO/AIA/02 is for utility applications in certain situations. When filing a continuing application, a copy of an earlier oath/declaration may be used if it complies with rules effective for the continuing application. Non-English oaths/declarations require an English translation and a statement of accuracy unless in approved translations. See 35 U.S.C. 115, 37 CFR §§ 1.63 and 1.69.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees and entity status discounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Design applications require filing, search, and examination fees. Small entity (37 CFR § 1.27) or micro entity (37 CFR § 1.29) status reduces fees but requires assertions or signed certification forms (PTO/SB/15A, PTO/SB/15B for micro entity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small entity status may be established by a written assertion; micro entity discount requires signed certification before paying discounted fee. Consult current USPTO Fee Schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing process, filing receipt and initial checks
rubrics_metrics.description: When an application with at least a specification, a drawing and a claim is received, it is assigned an application number and filing date and a filing receipt is sent. Applicants should promptly check the filing receipt for accuracy (inventor names, benefit/priority claims recognized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow suggested application formats to avoid defects; ensure accurate information to avoid problems later. Applications are generally examined in order of filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination scope and possible actions by examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: Examination checks formal requirements, whether the design can be understood from the drawing disclosure, and compares claimed subject matter with prior art. Examiner may reject claims if disclosure is incomplete/indefinite, or if prior art shows unpatentable subject matter; objections to form (e.g., drawing disclosure) may be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office actions will detail objections/rejections and may suggest amendments; keep Office actions in applicant files and do not return them to the Office. See MPEP references for exam practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to Office actions (requirements for replies)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reply must be timely, in writing, and must distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors in the Office action and address every objection and/or rejection. General statements asserting patentability without explaining how the design is patentable over prior art do not comply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If examiner requires compliance with a requirement, reply must comply or specifically argue why compliance is not required. Include application number, group art unit number, filing date, name of examiner who prepared the most recent Office action, and title of invention in communications. Failure to reply timely results in abandonment; see extension options below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing, abandonment, and extension of time rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Reply periods run from the 'Date Mailed' on the Office action. If reply is not received before the deadline, the application will be considered abandoned. A reply may be filed within six months of the mail date with a petition for extension of time and the fee under 37 CFR § 1.17(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extension fees increase with length of time requested. An extension need not be obtained before submitting a reply; it may be mailed with the reply. Extensions are not available for responding to a 'Notice of Allowance and Fee(s) Due.' See MPEP 502 for correspondence deposit rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate of Mailing and proof of receipt
rubrics_metrics.description: To ensure a reply is not missed, attach a 'Certificate of Mailing' establishing the mailing date when using the U.S. Postal Service; it is not the same as Certified Mail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A suggested Certificate of Mailing format and example USPTO form PTO/SB/92 are provided. If a receipt is desired for any paper filed, include a stamped self-addressed postcard listing applicant name/address, application number, filing date, and types of papers submitted; the mailroom will stamp and return it as evidence of receipt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of address notification procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant changes mailing address after filing, the Office must be notified in writing; failure to do so may result in communications being mailed to the old address and possible abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notification of change of address should be a separate letter and a separate notification must be filed for each application (e.g., use form PTO/AIA/122).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsideration, final rejection, and appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: After submission of a reply, the application is reconsidered; the examiner may withdraw a rejection and allow the application or repeat the rejection and make it final. Applicant may appeal to the Patent Trial and Appeal Board after receiving a final rejection or after the claim has been rejected twice. Applicant may also file a new application (continuation) claiming benefit of the earlier filing date to continue prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider appeal or continuation strategies when faced with final rejections; follow PTAB appeal procedures after final action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation to use registered patent practitioner and Pro Se assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO recommends engaging a registered patent attorney or patent agent to file and prosecute applications, although a knowledgeable applicant may self-prosecute. The Office offers a Pro Se Assistance Program for additional help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because drawing disclosure quality and prosecution practice are critical, consider retaining a professional draftsperson and a registered practitioner; Pro Se assistance available as a resource.
